# Research brief: `java.security.MessageDigest` and the MessageDigestSpec "UnsafeAlgorithm" finding (MD5)

## Source limits

- I could not retrieve the rule file itself. The tool I had was web search only, and it returned no content from `raw.githubusercontent.com/.../MessageDigest.crysl`. So I cannot quote the matching clause from that source, and Question 4 is only partly answered (see below).
- Search results returned short excerpts, not full pages. Where I say a page "does not say" something, that means the excerpt I saw did not say it.
- The Oracle Javadoc excerpts below are mostly from JDK 8, 11, 21, 25 and 26. I did not confirm every sentence in every version.

## Q1. What `MessageDigest` governs, and what the finding refers to

**What the class governs**
- The JCA Reference Guide describes `MessageDigest` as an engine class designed to provide the functionality of cryptographically secure message digests such as SHA-256 or SHA-512. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
- The Javadoc defines the lifecycle:
  - `getInstance(String algorithm)` returns a MessageDigest object that implements the specified digest algorithm.
  - The overloads are `getInstance(String, String provider)` and `getInstance(String, Provider)`.
  - `update(...)` has overloads for a single byte, a byte array, and a `ByteBuffer`.
  - `digest()` completes the hash computation by performing final operations such as padding.
  - Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- `digest(byte[] input)` is documented as performing a final update on the digest using the specified array of bytes, then completing the digest computation. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- `digest(byte[] buf, int offset, int len)` is also documented there; it throws `DigestException`.

**What the finding refers to**
- The value is the algorithm-name `String` passed to `MessageDigest.getInstance(...)`, here `"MD5"`.
- The Javadoc says the name should be a standard Java Security name (such as "SHA-256"). The Standard Algorithm Names page lists `MD5` as a MessageDigest algorithm. Its description: The MD5 message digest algorithm as defined in RFC 1321. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- A finding of the form "expecting one of … but found MD5" therefore refers to the constant (or statically resolved) algorithm argument of the factory call. It does not refer to `update` or `digest`.
- The supplied detector message lists six spellings: `SHA-256`, `SHA-384`, `SHA-512`, `SHA256`, `SHA384`, `SHA512`. The rule description in the research input lists only the three hyphenated names. I could not reconcile this, because I could not read the current rule file. This is an unresolved discrepancy.
- Oracle's Standard Names page lists hyphenated `SHA-256`, `SHA-384` and `SHA-512` in its MessageDigest table. The excerpts I saw do not list unhyphenated spellings for MessageDigest. Whether a given provider accepts `SHA256` as an alias is not established by the sources I read.

## Q2. Documented correct usage and remediation

**What the Javadoc and JCA guide document**
- The JCA guide's examples use `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")`. The usage sequence is `update(...)` calls followed by `digest()`, or `update` calls followed by `digest(byte[] input)`. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/27/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
- `getInstance` throws `NoSuchAlgorithmException` if no Provider supports a MessageDigestSpi implementation for the specified algorithm.
- `MessageDigest.isEqual` is documented only as comparing two digests for equality, doing a simple byte compare.

**What the sources do not say**
- The `MessageDigest` Javadoc and JCA guide excerpts I retrieved do not describe MD5 or SHA-1 as unsafe. They also give no remediation for using them. Their examples use SHA-256.
- The JCA guide's wording ("cryptographically secure message digests") and its SHA-256 examples are the closest official guidance I found. I found no official statement that says "replace MD5 with X".

**Related, narrower Oracle material (not about `MessageDigest.getInstance`)**
- The JDK treats MD5 as weak in other subsystems. For example, JDK-8285873 (fix version 19) adds DES, DESede and MD5 to the jdk.security.legacyAlgorithms security property, so that keytool warns. Source: https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8285873
- The JDK 19 note describes that change as having minimal compatibility risk and being behavioral. It concerns a security property and tool warnings.
- `jdk.jar.disabledAlgorithms` can disable MD5-signed JARs (https://www.java.com/en/configure_crypto.html). `jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms` and `jdk.certpath.disabledAlgorithms` govern TLS and certificate paths (https://ops.java/security/articles/disabling-crypto-algorithms/).
- These sources do not say they block `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")`. They are unrelated to a plain application-level digest.

**Standards context (supplementary, not Java-specific)**
- NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2 says SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 are acceptable for all hash function applications. Source: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-131Ar2.pdf
- The excerpt did not show how it treats MD5.

## Q3. Compatibility when the algorithm is changed

**Platform support**
- JDK 8 Javadoc requires every Java platform implementation to support MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256. Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/MessageDigest.html and https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/StandardNames.html
- The JDK 17 Standard Names page lists the required MessageDigest algorithms as SHA-1 and SHA-256. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- The JDK 25 Javadoc and Standard Names show SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-384. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- SHA-256 is required across all versions I checked. SHA-384 is required in the JDK 25 pages I saw.
- SHA-512 is not in the "required" list in the versions I saw. It is listed as a standard name, and the Javadoc says to consult the release documentation for your implementation to see if any other algorithms are supported.
- MD5 is no longer in the required list in the JDK 17 and JDK 25 pages I saw. It remains a documented standard name.

**Persisted and wire formats**
- The `MessageDigest` Javadoc and JCA guide do not document persisted-format or wire-format compatibility. They also give no migration path between algorithms.
- Each algorithm has its own fixed output size. The JCA guide gives 32 bytes for SHA-256 and 64 bytes for SHA-512. Standard Names lists 160 bits for SHA-1 and 256 bits for SHA-256.
- Changing the algorithm therefore changes the digest bytes and their length. This follows from the specifications, not from any Oracle migration statement. I found no documented guidance on handling stored digests or digests exchanged with external parties.
- Under your policy, a persisted identifier, a cache key, a runtime discriminator, and an externally fixed contract each need their own evidence.

## Q4. What the CrySL rule itself says

Only partial answers are possible from secondary sources. I could not quote the current rule file.

**Rule structure (from CogniCrypt documentation)**
- Each rule has a `SPEC` clause naming a fully qualified class name, followed by OBJECTS, EVENTS, ORDER, CONSTRAINTS, REQUIRES and ENSURES blocks. Source: https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/
- Events are defined by their signatures, and the EVENTS section can bind parameters and return values that CONSTRAINTS then constrain. Sources: https://eclipse.dev/cognicrypt/documentation/crysl/ and the ECOOP 2018 paper at https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol109-ecoop2018/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10/LIPIcs.ECOOP.2018.10.pdf

**Older versions of the MessageDigest rule (not the current master file)**
- The arXiv CrySL paper reproduces Figure 10, the MessageDigest rule: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.00564
- The excerpt shows an event `d3: digest(hash, offset, length)` and `Digests := d1 | d2 | d3`.
